To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
systemic benzodiazepeines given before inescapible shock or escape testing eliminate the enhanced fear conditioning produced by inescable shock.
the interference with escape that follows IS is mediated by a DRN-dependent sensitization of fear conditioning and that this sensitization can be prevented by benzodiazepine administration.

benzodiazepine microinjected into DRN blocks both the enhancement of conditioned fear and interference with subsequent escape learning produced by inescable shock, whereas systemic benzodiazepam administration blocks only the enhanced conditioned fear.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the DRN in mediating interference with escape responding after exposure to IS.
the role that stress-induced changes in central noradrenergic activity play in the acquisition of fear conditioning and in the subsequent interference with escape learning.
the role of the benzodiazepine receptor system in the behavioral and neurochemical consequences of inescapable stress and the effects of benzodiazepam on escape behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

benzodiazepine action at the DRN is critical in the mediation of the effects of IS on fear and escape responding, and that the failure of systemic benzodiazapines to block the IS-produced interference with escape when given before testing can be attributed to a lack of action at the DR.

benzodiazepine drugs act at the level of the DRN to reduce the interference with escape that follows exposure to IS, but that this effect can be countered by the systemic administration of benzodizepine drugs that act at a site remote from the DRN.

the benzodiazepine antagonist blocks the effect of benzodiazapine on both the enhancement of conditioned fear and the interference with escape behavior, but only if administered before exposure to the stressor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
benzodiazepine action in the DRN is necessary and sufficient to block the effects of IS on fear conditioning and escape performance. (C) 2003 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

benzodiazepine receptors in the region of DRN are involved in both enhanced fear and interference with learning, but that systemic benzodazepines do not block interference with escape when given before testing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the benzodiazepine receptor is a promising therapeutic target for treating PTSD and other disorders of excessive fear.
the DRN is an important site of action for the anxiolytic effects of benzodiazapines.
the DRN is a critical target for the effects of benzodiazepamines on escape deficits and enhanced fear conditioning.
